WASHINGTON (TND) — The Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act is heading to the Senate after Republicans, and even a few Democrats, passed it in the House.
However, it will be an uphill battle in the Senate with the Democrat majority and President Joe Biden explicitly saying he would veto the bill if it got to his desk.
The SAVE Act blocks non-citizens from voting in federal elections.
But it's stirring up quite the controversy on both sides of the aisle.
The biggest argument against it is that there are already protections in place that prevent non-citizens from voting.
The Illegal Immigration Reform And Immigrant Responsibility Act Of 1996 blocks non-citizens from voting in federal elections, but House Republicans don't think its protections are substantial enough.
The SAVE Act goes a step further than the previous 1996 law by **requiring documented proof of citizenship** to register to vote in federal elections.
If it's written into law it’s going to bring some big changes to how voters register, how their identities are verified, and how voter lists are maintained and performed year after year.

Despite accusations of redundancy from Democrats, House Republicans argue there have been instances of non-citizens voting in the past, and it could become more prevalent with the influx of illegal migrants in recent years.
According to the Cato Institute, there have been instances where non-citizens illegally voted in federal elections, but most of them were accidents when people just checked the wrong box.
There’s no good evidence that those non-citizens voted in large enough numbers to shift the outcome of any previous federal elections or even change the number of electoral college votes.

According to a new report from Ballotpedia, voters in Idaho, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Kentucky, Missouri, South Carolina, Iowa, and Wisconsin will decide whether to add a prohibition on noncitizens voting to their state constitutions in November.
Seven states including Alabama, Arizona, Colorado, Florida, Louisiana, North Dakota, and Ohio already include language blocking noncitizen voting.
It's not just changes to state constitutions, Indiana and Tennessee have new laws to check for and remove noncitizens while conducting voter list maintenance activities.
Minnesota requires a voter to be a U.S. citizen to vote an absentee ballot.
Noncitizens can vote in local elections in Washington, DC, and certain California, Maryland, and Vermont municipalities.
